introduction.p: We will describe the matrix transformation T that reflects 2-dimensional vectors across the horizontal axis. For instance, illustrates how a vector \xvec is reflected onto the vector T(\xvec).

image.shortdescription: A two dimensional vector and its reflection across the horizontal axis.

description.p: The vector \xvec=\twovec32 and its reflection across the horizontal axis T(\xvec)=\twovec3{-2}.

figure.caption: A vector \xvec and its reflection T(\xvec) across the horizontal axis.

statement.p: If \xvec = \twovec{2}{4}, what is the vector T(\xvec)? Sketch the vectors \xvec and T(\xvec).
More generally, if \xvec=\twovec{x}{y}, what is T(\xvec)?
Find the vectors T\left(\twovec{1}{0}\right) and T\left(\twovec{0}{1}\right).
Use your results to write the matrix A so that T(\xvec) = A\xvec. Then verify that T\left(\twovec{x}{y}\right) agrees with what you found in part b.

solution.p: We have the matrix A=\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp -1 \\ \end{array}\right]. It follows that T\left(\twovec{x}{y}\right) = A\twovec{x}{y} = \twovec{x}{-y} as expected.

statement.p: Describe the transformation that results from composing T with itself; that is, what is the transformation T\circ T? Explain how matrix multiplication can be used to justify your response.

solution.p: If we reflect a vector twice in the horizontal axis, we obtain the original vector. The matrix for the transformation T\circ T is simply AA= A^2 = \left[\begin{array}{rr}1\amp 0 \\ 0 \amp 1 \\ \end{array}\right].
